etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English gobben (“to drink or swallow greedily”), of uncertain origin +‎ -le (frequentative suffix). Middle English gobben is perhaps an alteration of Middle English globben (“to gulp down”), related to English gulpen (“to gulp”). However, compare also French gober.

definitions.definition: To eat hastily or greedily; to scoff or scarf (often used with up)

quote.text: Nowadays, he was lucky if his mam's auld drinking cronies gave him a gobble.

definitions.definition: (rare) An act of eating hastily or greedily.

quote.text: […]  wrinkling his forehead and moving his jaws and throat violently, as if he expected to choke with each gobble.

definitions.definition: (golf) A rapid straight putt so strongly played that, if the ball had not gone into the hole, it would have gone a long way past.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Onomatopoetic of the sound of a turkey.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) Of a turkey, to make its characteristic vocalisation; also, used of certain other birds.

quote.citation: 1886, Peter Christen Asbjørnsen, translated by H.L. Brækstad, Folk and Fairy Tales, page 72:
quote.text: Not before this performance is over does he [a male capercaillie] settle down to play, and commence gobbling and snapping his beak.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To make the sound of a turkey.

quote.citation: 1774, Oliver Goldsmith, History of the Earth and Animated Nature:
quote.text: He  […]  gobbles out a note of self-approbation.

definitions.definition: The sound of a turkey; or, a similar vocalisation of another bird.

quote.citation: 1886, Peter Christen Asbjørnsen, translated by H.L. Brækstad, Folk and Fairy Tales, page 86:
quote.text: But while the hen continued her cackle he finished his first play, and had commenced the gobble of his second, when a twig cracked beneath my feet.
